questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a semiconductor conducts moderately
questions.learningObjective: explain that a semiconductor's conductivity is set by a carrier concentration between a metal's and an insulator's
questions.stem: Silicon is called a semiconductor because its conductivity at room temperature lies between a metal's and an insulator's. What sets that value?

options.text: The number of mobile charge carriers, far below a metal's but far above an insulator's
The strength of the covalent bonds alone, which is the same in a metal and in an insulator
options.misconception: blames the bonds alone and ignores how many carriers are free to move

options.text: The width of the energy gap, which is the only thing that matters and sets carriers aside
options.misconception: treats the band gap as the whole story and omits the carrier concentration

options.text: The number of valence electrons, which is the same in every group four solid formed
options.misconception: counts valence electrons without noticing they stay bound in a semiconductor

questions.explanation: Conductivity in a solid comes from carriers that are free to move rather than from atoms that are bound in place, and in silicon at room temperature thermal energy excites only a tiny fraction of the valence electrons across the band gap. A metal has a partly filled band, so it has as many carriers as atoms and conducts excellently, while an insulator has a gap so wide that essentially nothing is excited and it conducts not at all. Silicon sits between those two because a small but non-zero carrier population is available to carry charge.
questions.hint: Ask how many charge carriers are free to move, since the bound atoms cannot conduct.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Origin of an electron and hole pair
questions.learningObjective: describe how thermal excitation of a valence electron creates one electron and one hole
questions.stem: In a pure semiconductor, free electrons and holes are always produced in equal numbers. Where does each such pair come from?

options.text: A valence electron is excited across the band gap, leaving a hole in the filled band
Two electrons are pulled out of the atomic cores and both become free charge carriers
options.misconception: describes ionising atoms, which gives ions rather than an electron and a hole

options.text: A bound electron is captured by a donor atom, and the ion it leaves becomes the hole
options.misconception: credits a donor impurity, which belongs in a doped sample instead

options.text: The lattice itself is ionised by the thermal motion, releasing matched positive ions
options.misconception: treats the process as ionising the lattice instead of exciting valence electrons

questions.explanation: A group four atom brings four valence electrons, which just fill its share of the bonds with its neighbours, and that full band has nowhere to accept another electron. Promote one of those bound electrons across the gap and the conduction band gains a free electron while the valence band gains a vacancy, and it is that vacancy that behaves as a positive carrier and is called a hole. The pair is created together, which is why the two concentrations are always equal in a pure sample, and doping adds carriers of one kind without adding the other.
questions.hint: An electron leaving a full band takes a slot with it, and the empty slot is the hole.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What a group five donor contributes
questions.learningObjective: state that a group five dopant supplies one free electron to the conduction band
questions.stem: Silicon is doped with an element from group five of the periodic table. What becomes of the fifth valence electron each dopant atom brings?

options.text: It is surplus to the four bonds needed, so it enters the conduction band as a carrier
It joins a fifth covalent bond, so the lattice is held more tightly than before
options.misconception: assumes the extra electron strengthens the bonds rather than freeing itself

options.text: It leaves the dopant entirely and is captured by a neighbouring silicon atom
options.misconception: describes electron capture, which is what an acceptor does instead

options.text: It remains in the valence band and so lowers the excitation needed for the next one
options.misconception: keeps the electron bound, which is exactly what a donor does not do

questions.explanation: Silicon needs four neighbours to complete its bonds, and a group five element arrives with one electron too many, so there is no fifth bond available for it to enter. Left in the conduction band, that electron has no bound state to fall back into and moves freely through the crystal, which is why the dopant is called a donor and why the material it produces is n-type. The dopant atom itself stays in the lattice as a fixed positive ion once it has given the electron away, and it is that fixed charge which keeps the electrons available to be collected.
questions.hint: Four bonds are already full, so ask what a fifth valence electron has left to do.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Majority carrier in n-type material
questions.learningObjective: identify electrons as the majority carriers in n-type material and give their sign
questions.stem: A sample of silicon has been doped with a group five element. Which carrier dominates in it, and what is the sign of that carrier?

options.text: Electrons, which are negative, because the donated carriers outnumber the generated holes
Holes, which are positive, because every donor atom leaves a positive ion behind
options.misconception: calls the fixed donor ions the majority carriers although they cannot move

options.text: Electrons, which are negative, because acceptor atoms outnumber the donor atoms
options.misconception: reverses the dopant group and puts acceptors into a donor-doped sample

options.text: Holes, which are positive, because doping raises the rate of pair generation
options.misconception: credits doping with creating extra pairs, which it does not do on its own

questions.explanation: Every donor atom contributes one free electron, and a doping level chosen to be useful is many orders of magnitude above the intrinsic concentration, so the donated electrons are the majority carrier and the thermally generated holes are a negligible minority. Since an electron is negative, n-type material carries current mainly in the negative sense. The positive ions left behind are fixed in the lattice and cannot move, so they are not carriers at all, and doping changes the carrier counts without changing the rate at which pairs are generated thermally.
questions.hint: Compare the number of carriers each dopant supplies with the intrinsic concentration.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Majority carrier in p-type material
questions.learningObjective: identify holes as the majority carriers in p-type material and their direction of drift
questions.stem: A trivalent element is added to silicon. What is the majority carrier in the resulting material, and which way does it drift in a field?

options.text: Holes, which drift towards lower potential as though positive charges moved there
Electrons, which drift towards higher potential as though negative charges moved there
options.misconception: picks electrons for a material whose acceptors leave holes as carriers

options.text: Holes, which drift towards higher potential as though positive charges moved there
options.misconception: reverses the drift that a positive carrier follows in an electric field

options.text: Electrons, which stay bound to the trivalent atoms and so carry no current at all
options.misconception: supposes the carriers are bound to the impurity and cannot conduct

questions.explanation: A trivalent atom has only three valence electrons, so it can form only three of the four bonds silicon needs and is left with an unfilled slot in the valence band. An electron from a neighbouring silicon atom drops into that slot, and the vacancy it leaves behind is the mobile positive carrier, which is why the material is p-type. A hole is a region of missing negative charge, so in an electric field it moves the way a positive charge would, that is down the potential, while the electrons that keep hopping into the vacancies drift the other way.
questions.hint: A missing electron is a positive vacancy, and a positive carrier follows the field.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The depletion region at a junction
questions.learningObjective: describe the depletion region as a carrier-free barrier held by fixed ionised dopants
questions.stem: One piece of doped silicon is n-type and another is p-type, and the two are brought into contact. What appears at the boundary?

options.text: A region stripped of mobile carriers, with fixed ions of both signs holding the barrier field
A neutral region where electrons and holes mix freely and recombine without limit
options.misconception: assumes the carriers survive the join instead of recombining across it

options.text: A conducting bridge of metallic silicon formed where the two pieces were joined
options.misconception: invents a metallic phase at the boundary instead of a carrier-free barrier

options.text: A stack of alternating donor and acceptor layers repeating the doping pattern
options.misconception: pictures a repeating layered structure rather than a single barrier region

questions.explanation: As soon as the two pieces touch, the large concentration difference drives electrons one way and holes the other, and where they meet they recombine, so the carriers are swept out of a region around the boundary. What is left there is the immobile skeleton of donor and acceptor ions, negative on the n-side and positive on the p-side, and the field between them is what stops further carriers crossing. That carrier-free region is the depletion region, and its built-in field is exactly the barrier a diode has to overcome before it conducts.
questions.hint: Ask what is left behind once the carriers have crossed and annihilated one another.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Forward and reverse bias of a diode
questions.learningObjective: state that forward bias lowers a junction barrier and reverse bias raises it
questions.stem: A p-n junction diode can be connected in two ways. How do the two bias arrangements differ in what they do to the barrier?

options.text: Forward bias lowers the barrier for majority carriers; reverse bias raises it and nearly stops them
Forward bias raises the barrier and blocks the current; reverse bias lowers it and lets carriers cross
options.misconception: reverses the action of the bias, blocking the junction where it should conduct

options.text: Both arrangements pass a substantial current, and only the type of carrier differs between them
options.misconception: denies rectification, so the diode would pass current either way round

options.text: Forward bias depends on the majority carriers, while reverse bias is set by the supply alone
options.misconception: removes the junction barrier from the reverse case entirely

questions.explanation: Forward bias connects the p-side to the positive terminal, which pushes the depletion region's built-in field the other way and narrows it, so the majority carriers face a much smaller barrier and a large current flows once the applied voltage approaches the diode's forward threshold. Reverse bias connects the p-side to the negative terminal, which reinforces the built-in field, widens the depletion region and pushes the carriers further apart, leaving only the tiny current carried by thermally generated minority carriers. That asymmetry in one device is what allows it to rectify.
questions.hint: Ask whether the applied bias pushes the depletion field or opposes it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Current below the forward threshold
questions.learningObjective: explain that a diode passes a small current below the forward threshold that rises exponentially above it
questions.stem: A silicon diode is said to need roughly 0.7 V forward before it passes a useful current. What is the circuit doing below that value?

options.text: Passing a very small current that rises steeply once the barrier is surmounted
Passing no current at all until the threshold, then the full current appears at once
options.misconception: treats the characteristic as a step rather than an extremely steep curve

options.text: Already passing half the supply voltage as current, well below the stated threshold
options.misconception: invents a linear current that the diode's characteristic never shows

options.text: Limiting the current by the series resistor alone, with the junction playing no part
options.misconception: blames the resistor while ignoring the junction's own barrier

questions.explanation: Nothing about the junction switches on at a chosen voltage; the current follows an exponential in the applied voltage, so it is already present at a fraction of a volt but far too small to register. Near 0.7 V the curve is so steep that the current climbs by roughly a factor of ten for every 60 mV or so, and the resistor in series is what fixes how much current flows once the diode's own resistance has become small. Describing the diode as blocked below the threshold is a shorthand for a current too small to matter, not for a current of exactly zero.
questions.hint: The characteristic is an exponential, not a switch, so ask how steep it is near 0.7 V.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Reverse breakdown of a diode
questions.learningObjective: describe reverse breakdown as a steep current rise that damages an ordinary diode
questions.stem: A reverse-biased diode is operated well beyond its maximum rated reverse voltage. How does it behave in that region?

options.text: The reverse current rises steeply, the device heats, and it may be damaged for good
The reverse current stays at its tiny saturation value however large the voltage becomes
options.misconception: assumes the saturation current cannot grow however far past the rating it goes

options.text: The diode changes polarity and begins passing forward current at the reverse voltage
options.misconception: believes the device flips into conduction like a breakover device

options.text: The reverse current falls to zero because the widening barrier suppresses the carriers
options.misconception: expects the barrier to suppress the current in the breakdown region itself

questions.explanation: Below the breakdown voltage the depletion region simply widens and the current stays at the tiny minority-carrier value. Once the field is strong enough to pull carriers out of the lattice by other means, the current jumps by orders of magnitude, and because the voltage across the device is then fixed, that power turns into heat inside a small package. An ordinary diode given this treatment is destroyed, which is why a diode chosen to work in this region is a different device with a controlled knee and a modest current rating.
questions.hint: Ask what the current does once the field becomes strong enough to free carriers directly.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Role of a zener diode
questions.learningObjective: state that a zener regulates by holding a constant voltage in reverse breakdown
questions.stem: A zener diode is connected in reverse across a load, fed through a series resistor from a higher supply. What is its job in that circuit?

options.text: To hold a chosen voltage on the load by passing a controlled reverse current in breakdown
To block the reverse direction and pass current forward, exactly as an ordinary diode does
options.misconception: treats it as a plain rectifier with no breakdown behaviour of its own

options.text: To smooth the ripple of the supply by charging and discharging over each ripple cycle
options.misconception: confuses voltage regulation with the smoothing done by a reservoir capacitor

options.text: To drop a steady 0.7 V in the forward direction as the supply's series element
options.misconception: confuses the breakdown knee voltage with the forward drop of silicon

questions.explanation: A zener is designed to break down at a precise voltage and to keep roughly that voltage as its current changes, so held in reverse across a load it pins the load voltage while the excess current goes through the series resistor and the device. That is different from using it forward, where it behaves like any other diode with a 0.7 V drop, and different again from a reservoir capacitor, whose job is to smooth ripple rather than to set a level. The series resistor is what makes the arrangement safe, since it limits the current once the zener starts conducting.
questions.hint: Ask what the device does once the reverse voltage reaches its knee value.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Ripple from an unsmoothed rectifier
questions.learningObjective: state that an unsmoothed half-wave rectifier delivers a large ripple at the supply frequency
questions.stem: A half-wave rectifier feeds a resistive load directly, with no smoothing capacitor anywhere in the circuit. What is the ripple on the output like?

options.text: Large, at the supply frequency, because the output falls to zero every half cycle
Absent, because the diode passes only the positive half of the incoming wave
options.misconception: assumes blocking the negative half cycle also removes the variation

options.text: Small, at twice the supply frequency, because the diode blocks the negative half cycle
options.misconception: gives the doubled frequency that belongs to a full-wave rectifier

options.text: Present at twice the supply frequency, since each half cycle is smoothed by the diode
options.misconception: pairs the doubled frequency with a smoothing action the circuit lacks

questions.explanation: A single diode passes the positive half of each cycle and blocks the negative half, so the load current falls to zero for half of every period and the output sits at the mean value during that time. The result is a large pulsating waveform whose repetition rate is the supply frequency itself, not twice it, since only one hump is produced per cycle. It is a full-wave rectifier that repeats at twice the supply frequency, because it produces two humps per incoming cycle, and even then the ripple is large unless a capacitor fills the gaps.
questions.hint: Count the humps produced per cycle of the incoming alternating supply.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: How a filter capacitor smooths
questions.learningObjective: explain that a reservoir capacitor smooths by charging at the peak and discharging through the load
questions.stem: A capacitor is placed across the load of a rectifier to smooth the output voltage. By what mechanism does it work?

options.text: It charges at each peak and discharges through the load between peaks, filling the gaps
It blocks the ripple frequency completely while passing the direct component to the load
options.misconception: treats the capacitor as a perfect filter rather than a store that drains

options.text: It converts the ripple into direct current at the same frequency as it arrives
options.misconception: describes a frequency conversion that a passive capacitor cannot perform

options.text: It cancels the ripple by driving an equal and opposite current through the load
options.misconception: describes active cancellation, which a passive component cannot arrange

questions.explanation: The rectified output reaches a maximum on each cycle, and the capacitor charges to that peak almost instantly because the diode conducts only during the brief interval when the diode is more conducting than the load path. Between peaks no current arrives, so the capacitor discharges into the load, and that stored charge is what holds the voltage up across the gap. The output is therefore a ripple riding on a level near the peak, and the ripple gets smaller as the capacitor is made larger, because a larger store drains more slowly over the same interval.
questions.hint: Think of the capacitor as a store that is filled at the peak and emptied between peaks.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Cost of a larger smoothing capacitor
questions.learningObjective: trade reduced ripple against higher peak diode current when sizing a reservoir capacitor
questions.stem: Enlarging the smoothing capacitor of a rectifier reduces the ripple on the output. What happens to the peak current the diodes must supply as the capacitor grows?

options.text: It rises, because the larger store draws a longer and larger charging pulse each cycle
It falls, because the longer discharge leaves the diodes conducting for less time
options.misconception: believes a bigger reservoir also reduces the peak charging current, which it raises

options.text: It is unchanged, since the peak diode current is set by the ripple and not by the capacitor
options.misconception: separates the ripple and the peak current as though they were independent

options.text: It vanishes, since the capacitor takes all the current and the diodes never conduct again
options.misconception: denies that a reservoir draws any charging current from the diodes

questions.explanation: A larger capacitor is replenished from a lower voltage, since the previous peak has fallen further before the next one arrives, so more charge has to be put back in a shorter time near the crest. That makes both the pulse longer in duration and larger in area, and the peak current the diodes carry rises with it. The trade is therefore real: a bigger capacitor buys less ripple from the load at the price of harder switching for the diodes and a larger transformer, which is why ripple and peak current are quoted together when a supply is designed.
questions.hint: Ask how much charge has to be restored, and over how much of the cycle it arrives.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Heat dissipated in a series regulator
questions.learningObjective: identify the dropped voltage times the current as the power a series regulator turns into heat
questions.stem: A series regulator is fed from a higher voltage than the one it delivers to its load. What sets the power it turns into heat?

options.text: The voltage dropped across the device multiplied by the load current flowing through it
The whole input voltage multiplied by the load current, since all of it crosses the device
options.misconception: attributes the entire input power to the device and forgets the useful output

options.text: The delivered output voltage multiplied by the load current, since useful work also heats
options.misconception: treats the useful output power as though it were the loss in the device

options.text: The ripple voltage multiplied by the load current, since ripple is the only loss present
options.misconception: credits the ripple as the sole loss, which is not where the heat comes from

questions.explanation: A series regulator works by dropping whatever excess the supply offers, so the voltage across the device is the input voltage less the output voltage, and the current through it is the load current. Their product is the power the device must shed, and a linear regulator is often limited far more by that heat than by its ability to pass the current, which is why a dropping voltage left in the circuit is a design fault rather than a detail. A switching regulator avoids the heat by storing the energy in an inductor and delivering it in pulses instead.
questions.hint: The loss is what the device removes from the supply, not what the load receives.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Operating a photodiode
questions.learningObjective: state that a photodiode is reverse biased and its current tracks the light on it
questions.stem: A photodiode is used as the sensor in a light meter. How is the device operated, and what does its output depend on?

options.text: It is reverse biased, and the current it generates grows with the light falling on it
It is forward biased, and its forward current falls as the light on it increases
options.misconception: uses forward bias and a decrease, neither of which describes a reverse cell

options.text: It is reverse biased, and the current through it is set by the reverse voltage alone
options.misconception: keeps the bias but removes the light dependence, which is the whole purpose

options.text: It is left unbiased, so it absorbs light and releases it again as visible output
options.misconception: treats the device as a light source rather than a detector when left alone

questions.explanation: Light falling on the device creates free carriers in the depletion region, and the reverse bias that normally suppresses the current now collects them, so the current flowing backwards is a direct measure of the illumination. The bias has to be there because without it the generated carriers simply recombine before they can be collected, and the current would not be usable. The relationship is close to linear over a working range, which is why a light meter can turn the current into a reading without a complicated correction.
questions.hint: Ask which bias lets the light-generated carriers be collected instead of recombining.

questions.topic: Why an indicator needs a series resistor
questions.learningObjective: explain that a series resistor drops the supply voltage the diode does not use and limits the current
questions.stem: A red indicator lamp is driven from a 5.0 V supply through a resistor in series with the diode. Why can the diode not simply be connected across the supply?

options.text: The diode holds its own forward voltage, and the resistor drops the rest and limits the current
The diode needs the whole supply applied to it, so any series element would rob it of voltage
options.misconception: assumes the diode consumes the full supply rather than holding a fixed drop

options.text: The diode passes no current at all until a resistor forces some through it from outside
options.misconception: believes an ideal forward-biased diode draws nothing without help

options.text: The resistor sets the colour of the light, which the diode would otherwise be free to choose
options.misconception: attributes the emitted colour to the resistor rather than to the material

questions.explanation: A light-emitting diode holds a forward voltage of a couple of volts, fixed by the energy gap of its material, and its current rises extremely steeply once that voltage is exceeded. Connected straight across 5.0 V it would have nothing to limit that current, so it would draw far more than it can carry and destroy itself. The series resistor takes the remaining volts and, since the current through it and the diode must be the same, it sets the current at a safe value, and the colour comes from the material chosen rather than from the resistor.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Hole concentration from the mass action law
questions.learningObjective: use the product of the electron and hole concentrations to find the minority carrier density
questions.stem: In a semiconductor the product of the electron and hole concentrations equals the square of the intrinsic concentration. With an intrinsic concentration of 1.5e10 per cubic metre and a measured electron concentration of 2.0e12 per cubic metre, what is the hole concentration in carriers per cubic metre? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The square of the intrinsic concentration is 1.5e10 times 1.5e10, which is 2.25e20 per cubic metre squared, and the hole concentration is that divided by the electron concentration, so 2.25e20 over 2.0e12 gives 1.125e8 per cubic metre. Checking the product directly, 2.0e12 times 1.125e8 is 2.25e20, which is the value the law requires, so the answer is consistent. The holes are four orders of magnitude below the intrinsic value, which is what marks this as a doped sample whose majority carriers are the electrons.
questions.hint: Divide the square of the intrinsic concentration by the measured electron concentration.

The intrinsic concentration near 1.0e10 per cubic metre is a million times smaller, so the thermally generated holes add nothing measurable and the electron figure is set entirely by the doping. Using the intrinsic value instead would describe an undoped sample rather than this one.

questions.topic: Resistivity from a measured resistance
questions.learningObjective: obtain the resistivity of a semiconductor from a measured resistance and its geometry
questions.stem: A sample of doped silicon is 2.0 cm long with a cross-section of 1.0 square millimetre, and it measures 20 ohm between its ends. What is its resistivity in ohm metres? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The resistivity is the resistance times the area divided by the length, so 20 ohm times 1.0e-6 square metres over 0.020 m gives 1.0e-3 ohm metres. Taking the resistance per unit length first gives the same figure: 20 ohm over 0.020 m is 1000 ohm per metre, and multiplying that by the 1.0e-6 square metre cross-section again gives 1.0e-3 ohm metres. The units work out because ohms times square metres over metres is ohms times metres, as a resistivity must be.
questions.hint: Use resistivity equals resistance times area over length, watching the unit conversions.

questions.topic: Forward current from the diode equation
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the diode equation at a stated forward voltage
questions.stem: A silicon diode has a saturation current of 1.0e-12 A and an ideality factor of 2, and at 300 K its thermal voltage is taken as 0.026 V. What current in amperes flows when the forward voltage is 0.60 V? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The current is the saturation current times the exponential of the voltage over the ideality factor times the thermal voltage, less one, and the exponent here is 0.60 over 2 times 0.026, which is 11.54. The exponential of 11.54 is 1.03e5, so the current is 1.0e-12 times 1.03e5, or 1.03e-7 A, which rounds to the 1.0e-7 A keyed here. Leaving out the ideality factor would halve the exponent and give a current smaller by a factor of about 300, which is the single most common slip in this calculation.
questions.hint: Divide the voltage by the ideality factor times the thermal voltage before taking the exponential.

questions.topic: Current in a resistor-loaded diode
questions.learningObjective: find the current in a diode and series resistor from the supply and the forward drop
questions.stem: A 6.0 V supply drives a silicon diode of 0.70 V forward drop in series with a 1.0 kilohm resistor. What current in amperes flows? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The resistor has to drop whatever the diode does not use, so the voltage across it is 6.0 V less 0.70 V, which is 5.30 V, and the current is 5.30 V over 1000 ohm, or 5.30e-3 A. Adding the two voltages back checks the loop: 0.70 V plus 5.30e-3 A times 1000 ohm, which is 5.30 V, gives the 6.0 V supply. Using the full supply voltage across the resistor would give 6.0e-3 A, which assumes the diode drops nothing at all.
questions.hint: Subtract the diode's forward drop from the supply before dividing by the resistance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Current through a zener regulator
questions.learningObjective: find the zener current as the difference between the series and load currents
questions.stem: A 12.0 V supply feeds a 5.0 V zener through a 1.0 kilohm resistor, and the load draws 4.0 mA. What current in amperes flows through the zener? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The resistor carries whatever the supply provides once the zener has taken its 5.0 V, so the current in it is 7.0 V over 1000 ohm, which is 7.0e-3 A, and the same current then splits between the zener and the load. The zener therefore carries 7.0e-3 A less the 4.0e-3 A drawn by the load, which is 3.0e-3 A. questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a reverse-biased diode still conducts
questions.learningObjective: explain minority-carrier leakage in reverse bias and the consequence of raising the bias into breakdown
questions.stem: A reverse-biased diode is often described as an open circuit in a circuit diagram. Explain in your own words why a small current still flows, and what happens when the reverse bias is raised far enough.

answer.exemplar: The open-circuit symbol is a shorthand for a very large resistance, not for an infinite one, and two effects keep a small current flowing. Thermal energy generates electron and hole pairs right through the sample all the time, and the reverse bias sweeps the minority carriers that reach the depletion region across it, giving a reverse current set by how fast pairs are generated rather than by the voltage across the device. That is why the reverse characteristic is almost flat, and it is also why a diode's leakage rises steeply with temperature, since generation depends on temperature. Raise the reverse voltage far enough and a different mechanism takes over: the field at the barrier becomes strong enough to pull carriers out of the lattice directly, the current climbs by orders of magnitude, and the power dissipated in a small package destroys the junction. Between those two regimes the reverse current is small enough to ignore for signal work, which is exactly what the open-circuit symbol is telling you.

questions.explanation: The symbol stands for a very large resistance, not an infinite one, and the residual current is minority carriers swept the wrong way by the field. Beyond a certain voltage a different mechanism takes over and the current rises steeply.
questions.hint: Ask which carriers supply the small reverse current, and then what happens when the field becomes strong enough to free more of them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a switch is driven into saturation
questions.learningObjective: explain the choice of saturation for a switching transistor and the gain given up by overdriving it
questions.stem: Explain why a transistor used as a switch is driven past the edge of its amplifying region into saturation, and what a designer gives up by doing so.

answer.exemplar: A switch has only two jobs to do, hold the load off and hold it on, so the device is judged on the voltage it leaves across a load rather than on any gain. In the amplifying region the collector voltage falls in proportion to the base current, and since the current gain varies between individual transistors, with temperature and with the supply, the voltage that results from a given drive is not predictable. Driving the base harder and harder eventually pushes the collector voltage down to a couple of tenths of a volt and stops there, because the transistor can no longer raise the current however much base current it is given. That floor is saturation, and landing in it makes the output voltage a property of the circuit rather than of the transistor, so it is repeatable and the load is held firmly on. What is given up is exactly the property the device is prized for in a linear circuit: the gain. The base current has to be several times what the load needs, so a saturated switch draws more base power than a linear stage would, and it dissipates the excess as heat in the base junction. That is a fair trade for a switch and a poor one for an amplifier.

questions.explanation: Saturation puts a floor under the output voltage that depends on the circuit rather than on the transistor's gain, which is what makes a switch repeatable. The price is a base drive well beyond what the load needs.
questions.hint: Ask whether the output voltage should depend on the transistor's gain or on the circuit.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: How the ideal op-amp rules follow from high gain
questions.learningObjective: derive the zero input current and virtual short conditions from very high gain with negative feedback
questions.stem: Explain how the two conditions normally used when analysing an ideal operational amplifier follow from its very large gain and its negative feedback connection.

answer.exemplar: The amplifier's output responds to the difference between its two inputs, multiplied by a gain so large that a difference of microvolts would already swing the output from one rail to the other. On its own that would make the device useless, because the offset of a real input pair is much larger than a microvolt. What rescues it is the feedback path: some of the output is returned to the inverting input, so any output change moves that input against the change that produced it, and the loop settles only when the two inputs are equal to within a fraction of a microvolt. That near equality is the first of the two usual conditions, and it holds only while the amplifier is inside its linear range and the feedback is negative. The second follows from the same pair: with no current path into the input at all, whatever current arrives at that input has to continue through the feedback resistor, which is why the current through the input resistor equals the current through the feedback resistor and no loading appears. The two conditions are the whole of the analysis, and each one fails loudly in practice, the first by clipping at the rails and the second by an input bias current that has to be compensated.

questions.explanation: Very large gain alone would saturate on the input offset. Negative feedback forces the two inputs together to within a negligible voltage, and the absence of input current then fixes the current in the feedback path.
questions.hint: Ask what must be true of the two input voltages before a huge gain can give a moderate output.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Static power in a CMOS inverter
questions.learningObjective: explain why a settled complementary inverter draws no static current, contradicting the claim of continuous conduction
questions.stem: A student claims that a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor inverter passes a steady current from the positive supply to ground at all times, and that this steady current is why its output is slow. Explain in your own words why the circuit configuration contradicts the claim.

answer.exemplar: Look at what the two transistors are actually doing. The p-channel device at the top and the n-channel device at the bottom are in series between the supplies, with their drains joined at the output, and their gates are tied together to the input. When the input is high the p-channel device is off and the n-channel device is on, and when the input is low the roles swap. In either settled state one of the two is off, and an off device presents a very large resistance, so there is no continuous path from one supply to the other and the static current is close to zero. The output node is therefore left holding its charge rather than being discharged through a path, which is the opposite of the student's conclusion: the output changes quickly because almost nothing is loading it. Current does flow during the short interval when the input moves, because for part of the transition both devices conduct, and that brief current is the cost of charging and discharging the load capacitance. It is the switching current, and the energy in it, that sets the power of a working circuit, not any steady flow while nothing is happening. A complementary pair is used precisely for this reason, since the static power of a logic family is what limits how much it can be packed onto a chip.

questions.explanation: In a settled state one of the two series devices is off, so there is no path for a steady current, and an unladen output node is exactly what makes the change fast.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two series devices is off in each of the two settled states.
